result.source_concept: Bookshelf organization (physically arranging books by height)

mappings.target_element: Selecting a pivot element in the array
mappings.relation: Both serve as a reference point for partitioning
mappings.evidence: You pick one book as the "pivot" (like a reference point).

mappings.source_element: Splitting books into two piles: shorter than the pivot and taller than the pivot
mappings.target_element: Partitioning the array into elements less than and greater than the pivot
mappings.relation: Both create two subproblems based on comparison to the pivot
mappings.evidence: You then split the books into two piles: one pile with books shorter than the pivot and another with books taller than the pivot.

mappings.source_element: Recursively applying the same process to each pile
mappings.relation: Both use recursion to handle smaller subproblems
mappings.evidence: Repeat the same process for each pile: pick a new pivot, split the books into smaller piles, and so on.

mappings.source_element: Base case when a pile has one or no books
mappings.target_element: Base case when a subarray has size 0 or 1
mappings.relation: Both define a termination condition for recursion
mappings.evidence: Each pile becomes so small (just one book or none) that no more sorting is needed.

mappings.source_element: Combining the piles back together in order
mappings.target_element: Concatenating the sorted subarrays after recursion
mappings.relation: Both produce the final sorted sequence by joining the results of subproblems
mappings.evidence: Finally, you combine all the piles back together in order.

result.process_summary: Both the bookshelf organizer and quicksort follow a divide‑and‑conquer process: select a pivot (reference book or array element), partition the set into two groups based on the pivot, recursively apply the same steps to each group until they are trivially small, and then assemble the sorted groups to obtain the final ordered collection.
potential_breaks: The analogy mentions an explicit "combine" step, which may suggest a merging operation not present in quicksort (quicksort simply concatenates the sorted partitions).
The bookshelf scenario sorts by physical height, whereas quicksort can sort any comparable key.
Physical constraints of a bookshelf (e.g., spatial layout) do not map to the abstract array representation used by quicksort.
